newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Izetbegovic appeals for Bosnian treaty compliance.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic appeals for Bosnian treaty compliance.

text.p: The Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency said on Monday his country was heading towards disintegration unless major powers took action to enforce the terms of a peace treaty.
In an appeal to international envoys, presidency chairman Alija Izetbegovic said Croat and particularly Serb authorities were violating the Dayton peace agreement with impunity.
"This is an invitation to undertake necessary measures, before it is too late," said a statement issued by Izetbegovic's office.

The international community needed to impose penalites, including the suspension of economic aid, on any party which failed to make good on its obligations under the U.S.-sponsored treaty signed in December 1995, the statement said.

Bosnian Serb authorities have failed to abide by arms control limits, violated human rights provisions, blocked the return of non-Serb refugees, refused to hand over indicted war criminals and tried to circumvent the country's peacetime constitution and sovereignty, it said.

The Serb entity, which together with the Moslem-Croat federation comprises post-war Bosnia, had flouted the peace treaty by unilaterally adopting laws on citizenship and signing a co-operation agreement with neighbouring Yugoslavia.
"The whole peace process has generally had a negative direction so far, which is leading to further disintegration of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
"This is endangering the foundations on which the peace was established," the statement said.
Izetbegovic delivered the warning to diplomats from the major powers' Contact Group on former Yugoslavia, and the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt.
He singled out Bildt for criticism, accusing the High Representative of tolerating violations of the treaty and allowing Serb or Croat authorities to reduce the authority of central governing bodies.
Bildt issued his own assessment of the peace process last week, warning that "creeping secessionism" by Serb or Croat authorities could undermine the Dayton accords which ended the 1992-95 war.
In a report to the U.N. Security Council, Bildt also called on Bosnian Moslems to show more willingness to share power under new joint institutions instead of merely paying "lip-service" to the idea.
He said the Moslems had failed to share out ambassadorial posts with their Croat and Serb rivals as they had agreed.
Izetbegovic's appeal follows speculation in Sarajevo media that frustrated Moslem leaders were giving up on the goal of a unifed Bosnia and were now considering carving out a state for Moslems.

Some political analysts say Izetbegovic and other Moslem leaders were merely testing the reaction of Western powers and trying to force them to pay more attention to Bosnia at a time when the international focus has shifted elsewhere.
